title: Agents reported thousands of bugs, how many were real? - Ian Butler and Nick Gregory

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk introduces SM-100, a benchmark for evaluating agents on software maintenance tasks, with design, metrics, and comparative performance results. SM-100 and Bismuth serve the coding assistant and developer platform domains for software engineering. The content centers on the evaluation and testing phase of AI agent development. Prerequisites include SDLC knowledge, agentic AI tooling familiarity, and static analysis benchmarking experience. This is a conference presentation at the AI Engineer event. All nine evidence anchors are directly cited from the transcript.

summary: Ian Butler and Nick Gregory of Bismuth present SM-100, a benchmark designed to evaluate autonomous agents on software maintenance tasks, an area underserved by existing benchmarks like HumanEval, Polyglot, and LiveCodeBench that focus on feature development. They argue that maintenance requires deeper system understanding than feature development, as finding bugs often demands more comprehensive knowledge of architecture and data flow than originally writing the feature. Existing bug detection benchmarks from the security space are limited by simplistic bug patterns, language bias (mostly Java), and a security-focused orientation that misses non-security defects. SM-100 addresses these gaps with 100 triaged, validated, and classified bugs from over 84 public repositories, spanning Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, and Go, ranging from obvious low-domain-knowledge bugs to senior staff-level engineering challenges. Only objective bugs are included—explicit security issues or logical issues causing data loss or system crashes—excluding ambiguous cases. Each bug is annotated with severity, context, required domain knowledge, difficulty, and implication. The benchmark yields four metrics: needle-in-haystack bug discovery, false positive rate, bug detection at introduction time, and remediation effectiveness. Performance comparisons reveal most popular agents score poorly on SM-100, with the highest non-Bismuth agent at only 7% true positive rate. Bismuth leads needle-in-haystack discovery with 10 bugs found versus the next best at 7. Open-source models R1 and Llama Maverick achieve only 1-2% true positive rates. Agents are narrow in their thinking, even when using thinking models, and don't go deep enough. On a per-run basis, total bug counts remain consistent but the specific bugs found change, indicating models don't evaluate files holistically. Despite 60-80% scores on SWE-bench, agents still struggle with SM-100, suggesting existing agents can create software upfront but struggle to manage and fix software after deployment. Bismuth runs on Anthropic models and beat Claude Code in multiple categories while improving on the base model.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Backgrounds
sections.summary: Ian Butler (CEO) and Nick Gregory (CTO) introduce themselves and Bismuth. Ian's background is in data engineering, ML, and search, previously at Zillow on AB testing and earlier building technical documentation search with Nick. Nick's background is in software security, formerly at Google on endpoint security and before that as a research scientist focused on detecting software exploitation. They acknowledge Base 10 for providing compute credits.

sections.title: Motivation: Gaps in Existing Benchmarks Across the SDLC
sections.summary: The speakers explain that existing benchmarks cover feature development and testing but neglect other SDLC phases. They argue maintenance requires deeper system reasoning than feature development, and agents struggle with holistic evaluation, finding only subsets of bugs while missing obvious ones and confirming spurious ones. Thinking models help somewhat but reasoning remains narrow.

sections.title: Limitations of Existing Bug Detection Benchmarks
sections.summary: Existing security-focused bug detection benchmarks are unsuitable for evaluating agentic AI because they focus on simplistic statically-findable bugs (null pointers, buffer overflows, SQL injection), are limited in language coverage (mostly Java), and are biased toward security issues while ignoring non-security defects like copy-paste bugs that still break software.

sections.title: SM-100 Benchmark Design and Bug Selection Criteria
sections.summary: SM-100 comprises 100 triaged, validated bugs from over 84 public repositories across Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, and Go. Only objective bugs—explicit security or logical issues causing data loss or crashes—are included. Each bug is annotated with severity, context, required domain knowledge, difficulty, and implication. Feature requests, optimization, style, and design decisions are excluded.

sections.title: Benchmark Metrics and Methodology
sections.summary: The benchmark produces four metrics: needle-in-haystack discovery, false positive rate, detection at bug introduction time, and remediation success. The needle-in-haystack methodology scopes agents to relevant subsystems containing files modified in the golden PR commit, avoiding both excessive search time and evaluation bias.

sections.title: Basic Agent Implementation Findings
sections.summary: Basic agent implementations with shell, search/replace, think, report bug, and finish tools found 5-6 bugs but had a 97% false positive rate. Agents built from standard model card or methodology releases are insufficient for production-quality bug detection.

sections.title: Performance Comparisons, Industry Findings, and Conclusion
sections.summary: Performance comparisons show Bismuth leads needle-in-haystack discovery with 10 bugs found versus next best at 7. True positive rates vary widely: Codex at 45%, Bismuth at 25%, Claude Code at 16%, while open-source models R1 and Llama Maverick achieve only 1-2%. The highest popular agent score outside Bismuth is 7% on SM-100. Devon, Cursor, and Cosign produced 900-1,300 reports with only 3-10% true positive rates. Agents exhibit narrow thinking even with thinking models, and per-run bug counts remain consistent while specific bugs found change, indicating lack of holistic file evaluation. Despite 60-80% scores on SWE-bench, agents struggle with SM-100, suggesting they can create software upfront but struggle to maintain and fix deployed software. Bismuth runs on Anthropic models and beat Claude Code in multiple categories. The speakers call for the industry to focus on maintenance tasks representing the back 90% of software engineering work.
